spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** **Database sharding** divides a logical table into horizontally disjoint subsets (shards), each hosted on an independent database primary with its own CPU, buffer pool, WAL, and NVMe storage.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Hash Partitioning with Virtual Nodes (vnodes) Across Physical Shards (S1#0 -> S2#0 -> S3#0 -> S1#1); Online Range Split & Epoch Fencing in Vitess / Citus (vtgate Router -> etcd Metadata -> Shard 11 [A0-AF] -> Shard 17 [A8-AF]).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Compare partitioning strategies across write balance, range-scan efficiency, and resharding mechanics. Use stateless proxy routers (`vtgate`, Citus coordinator) backed by etcd/Raft topology metadata, replace centralized `AUTO_INCREMENT` with UUIDv7/Snowflake IDs, and enforce.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore partition hotspot mitigation, distributed KV stores, unique ID generation, and Two-Phase Commit vs Sagas.

learningJourney.title: What is Database Sharding
learningJourney.explanation:
**Database sharding** divides a logical table into horizontally disjoint subsets (shards), each hosted on an independent database primary with its own CPU, buffer pool, WAL, and NVMe storage. Unlike read replicas—which copy 100% of data and only offload `SELECT` queries—sharding splits both reads and writes.

Two partitioning functions dominate: **Range partitioning** (CockroachDB, TiKV, HBase) maps contiguous key intervals (`[A-F]`, `[G-M]`) via a sorted boundary table, while **Hash partitioning** (DynamoDB, Cassandra, Vitess `xxhash64`) hashes keys onto a consistent hash ring or 1,024–4,096 virtual buckets.

sectionDiagram.title: Hash Partitioning with Virtual Nodes (vnodes) Across Physical Shards
sectionDiagram.summary: Virtual nodes spread key ranges evenly and ensure adding a physical shard moves only 1/N of buckets.

learningJourney.title: Why Single Primaries Hit a Wall (and How Epoch Routing Prevents Split-Brain)
learningJourney.explanation: Vertical scaling hits physical/economic walls around 64–128 vCPUs and NVMe IOPS saturation. When a PostgreSQL primary exceeds ~15k–25k write TPS or its B-tree indexes spill RAM, vacuum lag and lock contention degrade p99 across every tenant. During live shard splits, enforcing **routing epoch/generation numbers** prevents stale clients from writing to demoted shards.

sectionDiagram.title: Online Range Split & Epoch Fencing in Vitess / Citus
sectionDiagram.summary: Epoch fencing ensures a router with a stale shard map cannot cause split-brain writes after ownership moves.

comparison.choice: Shard: Write TPS / Index Size Exceeds Largest Primary
benefits: Linear write scaling when 95%+ of OLTP queries include `tenant_id` or `account_id`.
costs: Cross-shard joins and global secondary indexes require async CDC projections.

comparison.choice: Shard: Regulatory Data Residency (GDPR EU vs US)
benefits: Physically pins tenant rows to regional storage clusters.
costs: Requires geo-aware routing metadata and regional failover planning.

comparison.choice: Defer: <2–5 TB Dataset or Read-Only Bottleneck
benefits: Read replicas + covering indexes + Redis keep single-primary ACID joins intact.
costs: Premature sharding forces 2PC or Sagas on workflows that didn't need them.

learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: How to manage Shard Keys, Colocation & Global Indexes
learningJourney.explanation:
1. **Colocate Related Tables**: Shard `orders`, `order_items`, and `payments` by `merchant_id` so checkout commits in one local ACID transaction.
2. **Over-Provision Logical Shards**: Create 256–1,024 virtual buckets from day one even on 4 hosts.
3. **Prevent Tail Hotspots & Celebrity Skew**: Prefix monotonic keys with `tenant_id` or a 2-byte hash, and salt celebrity tenants (`tenant_id#0..7`).
4. **Async Global Secondary Indexes**: Maintain lookup tables (e.g., `email -> user_id`) via Debezium CDC (~50–200 ms eventual consistency).

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: Range vs. Hash vs. Composite vs. Directory
learningJourney.explanation: Compare partitioning strategies across write balance, range-scan efficiency, and resharding mechanics.

benefits: Fast ordered `BETWEEN` scans on 1–2 shards; splits 64 MB–1 GB ranges cleanly.
costs: Monotonic keys (`created_at`, `SERIAL`) create tail-shard write hotspots.

benefits: Uniform write distribution; adding a node moves only `1/N` vbuckets.
costs: Range scans scatter-gather across all shards, amplifying p99 tail latency.

benefits: Uniform across tenants AND fast time-range scans within a single tenant.
costs: Celebrity tenants still require sub-sharding or dedicated shards.

benefits: Arbitrary VIP placement and per-entity migration without rehashing.
costs: Adds a lookup hop on every query; directory becomes a critical SPOF.

learningJourney.purpose: The trade-off: compare competing approaches across latency, consistency, and operational cost.

learningJourney.title: Production Architecture: Proxy Router + Virtual Shards + Epoch Guard
learningJourney.explanation: Use stateless proxy routers (`vtgate`, Citus coordinator) backed by etcd/Raft topology metadata, replace centralized `AUTO_INCREMENT` with UUIDv7/Snowflake IDs, and enforce linter/ORM guards requiring the shard key on every OLTP query so scatter-gather stays rare.

ideas.title: Avoid 2PC on High-Throughput OLTP
ideas.description: If a 2PC coordinator crashes after `PREPARE`, shards hold row locks indefinitely. Prefer shard-key colocation or Transactional Outbox Sagas.

ideas.title: Scatter-Gather Tail Amplification
ideas.description: A query fanning out to 64 shards inherits the slowest shard's GC pause or compaction spike as its p99.

knowledgeCheck.question: A range-partitioned cluster keys an `events` table by `created_at` (monotonic timestamp), causing 100% of writes to hammer a single node. What fix distributes writes evenly while still keeping per-device time-range scans fast?

options.text: Use a composite shard key `(device_id, created_at)` (or hash-prefix + timestamp) so writes spread across all shards while each device's timeline stays contiguous
options.feedback: Correct: prefixing with high-cardinality `device_id` spreads writes across nodes while preserving range locality per device.
Pure `hash(event_id)` forces every device's 7-day time-range scan to scatter-gather across all shards.
Monotonically increasing numbers still land on the tail range.

_recommendedProblem.title: Design a Distributed Key-Value Store
_recommendedProblem.prompt: Design a distributed, highly available key-value store (Dynamo/Cassandra style) supporting `put(key, value)` (up to 1 MB) and `get(key)` at 10K sustained / 50K peak writes/sec and 100K reads/sec (~1 TB raw, 3 TB at N=3) with < 10 ms intra-DC p99 latency, tunable quorum (R, W, N), and automatic partition/node failure recovery.
